questions.title: Why does adding the value 0 to the ternary weights {-1, 0, 1} allow the representation to reach 1.58 bits instead of just 1 or 2 bits?
questions.question_body: The abstract states that BitNet b1.58 uses ternary weights {-1, 0, 1} and calls this '1.58 bits'. However, in standard information theory, a ternary state (3 levels) would occupy $\log_2(3) \approx 1.585$ bits. But isn't this mathematically just rounding $\log_2(3)$? I understand that the paper refers to it as '1.58', but is there a specific reason to stop at this decimal approximation? If I have a weight of -0.5 which rounds down to -1, does that mean I'm wasting half a bit's worth of information compared to a binary system where I can't represent that intermediate state? Can someone explain if '1.58 bits' is a precise theoretical claim or just a label for the ternary alphabet?

questions.title: How exactly does SORTFLOW's 'in-chip communication' optimize the memory transfer for sparse weights compared to full precision models?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that 1-bit LLMs enable better in-chip communication because they only store weights in SRAM (or on-chip memory) rather than transferring them from DRAM for every operation like full-precision LINEAR layers do. I see the argument that you load sparse tensors once and update them, but in a device like LINEAR which selects one existing weight per column at every step, isn't that still technically accessing weight memory many times (e.g., once per head/token)? How is accessing those weights inherently more expensive in terms of power and latency than accessing dense weights in SRAM? Is it primarily about the elimination of the DRAM bottleneck during initialization versus retrieval?

questions.title: What prevents directly encoding floating-point values across {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2} into ZNIST's ternary latent space without massive loss of expressivity?
questions.question_body: The intuition given is that by encoding floating-point vectors into SIGN-Magnitude latent space and then converting those vectors back via ZNIST to ternary vectors with {-2,-1,0,1,2}, we only incur loss on floating-point addition during latent processing. But why doesn't this approach simply work better with BINARY latent space (0 or 1 per dimension per token) instead of SIGN-Magnitude? If SIGN-Magnitude adds extra dimensions compared to BINARY (which only needs one bit per feature + sign), shouldn't SPECIFIC TO TOKEN activation loss be significantly lower with BINARY? Why is ZNIST specifically designed around SIGN-Magnitude here?

questions.title: Is an effective channel width of 'less than one Qubit' physically possible for hardware design based on the current state of charge control electronics?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions achieving this efficiency with an effective channel width much lower than one Qubit per tensor gate element given modern transistor technology developments like Simple FinFETs. I am struggling to reconcile this with energy scaling relations: hasn't single-electron tunneling current already become dominant in very small transistors (hence the low energy vs bandwidth trade-off)? If we are trying to reduce channel widths further below specific dimensions where single-electron effects dominate or introduce significant variability due to device-to-device fluctuations in charge storage control circuits, would noise and variability—not energy savings—become the limiting factor instead? How are trade-offs being managed when approaching sub-unit-cell geometries for weight storage?
